screens.title: AI Tasks and Blackboard: Making AI Smarter
screens.narratorSegment: Today we will take a patrol AI that feels rigid and make it responsive. The Blackboard is the AI's short-term memory — a shared place where the AI Controller, Behavior Tree, and perception systems store the values that matter in the moment, like a target actor or a target location. You'll learn how Blackboard Keys represent typed variables such as Vector, Object, Boolean, and Name, and why choosing the right key type matters. We'll also build a custom Behavior Tree Task in Blueprint that finds the player, writes their actor and location into the Blackboard, and then finishes cleanly so the Behavior Tree can continue. Finally, we'll modify a Behavior Tree to prioritize chasing the player using a Selector and a Blackboard decorator that checks if a target is set. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to create BB_EnemyAI, add keys, author a BTTask_BlueprintBase to update the Blackboard, and wire a chase-vs-patrol selector so AI behaves more naturally. Think about how a shared memory helps different systems coordinate without tight coupling — that's the core idea you'll use repeatedly.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › AI Tasks and Blackboard

AI Tasks and Blackboard

Make patrol AI responsive by using a shared Blackboard and custom Behavior Tree tasks authored in Blueprint.

In this lesson
Create BB_EnemyAI and keys; build a custom FindPlayer task; wire a chase selector.
Key artifact
BTT_FindPlayer (BTTask_BlueprintBase) that sets TargetActor and TargetLocation.
Outcome
AI that falls back to patrol but prioritizes chasing when target is set.
Why this matters

Using a Blackboard decouples detection, planning, and actions so systems can share facts without hard wiring. It makes AI modular and easier to debug.

Visual concept
Shared memory and task flow
Blackboard snapshot
TargetActor (Object)
Actor ref or None
TargetLocation (Vector)
World position
IsPlayerDetected (Boolean)
True / False
Explore Key Topics

Typed variables the AI uses to remember facts.
Custom Tasks
Blueprint tasks let you encapsulate game-specific logic.
Behavior Tree Flow
Selectors and decorators prioritize chase over patrol.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand why the Blackboard is the central shared memory for AI and how Blackboard Keys let you store typed facts like positions, actor references, and boolean states. You will be able to create and wire a Blackboard asset to a Behavior Tree, select the correct key types for your data, and use them inside tasks and decorators. You will also author custom Behavior Tree Tasks in Blueprint, implement their logic in Receive Execute AI, and correctly call Finish Execute so the tree continues. Finally, you will integrate these pieces to build a chase priority: the AI checks for a target, runs a custom task to populate Blackboard entries, then moves to the target; when the target is absent the AI resumes patrol. Each objective includes a brief competency milestone so you can confirm mastery by inspection and runtime testing. These skills will make your AI modular, debuggable, and ready for more advanced perception systems later on.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Verification & Pitfalls

Test and verify

Runtime checks ensure your Blackboard and tasks behave as intended while avoiding common errors.

Run checklist
  • Attach BB_EnemyAI to your Behavior Tree Root.
  • Open the Blackboard and Behavior Tree debugger in PIE.
  • Confirm TargetActor and TargetLocation update when detecting the player.
  • Ensure Finish Execute is called in your BTTask.
Common mistakes

Wrong key types, forgetting Finish Execute, and not binding the Blackboard to the Behavior Tree are the most frequent issues.

Quick debugging tips

Use a Delay during testing

Temporarily set TargetActor from Event BeginPlay with a short delay to observe the chase behavior immediately in PIE.

Naming convention

Clear key names like TargetActor and TargetLocation reduce confusion and make decorators easy to set up.

Key Takeaway

Testing early and verifying Blackboard values in the debugger will save time and reveal type or flow errors quickly.

screens.title: What is the Blackboard?
screens.narratorSegment: The Blackboard is best understood as a short-term memory store for an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree. It is an asset you create in the Content Browser, then populate with keys that describe facts the AI might need right now: where to move, which actor to chase, or whether a state flag is set. The power of the Blackboard comes from decoupling: perception components, tasks, decorators, and other Blueprints can all read from and write to the same set of keys without calling each other directly. For example, a perception component can set a TargetActor key when it sees the player; a custom task can later read that key and write TargetLocation; a Move To task can then use TargetLocation or TargetActor. A common misconception is to treat the Blackboard like a global game state — instead, treat it as short-lived, local memory scoped to an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree. Use clear naming and correct key types to avoid confusion. In practice, you'll create BB_EnemyAI, add Vector and Object keys, attach it to your Behavior Tree root, and then watch values change in the debugger as runtime evidence that systems are communicating correctly. How might you limit what you store in the Blackboard to avoid clutter?

keyIdea.text: A local, typed memory where AI systems publish and consume transient facts for decision-making.

content.html:
Core Concept What is the Blackboard?

Blackboard as shared memory

An asset with typed keys that Behavior Trees and Blueprints use to share state.

Definition

A Blackboard is an asset containing keys. It is intended for transient, per-controller memory used during decision making, not for permanent game state.

Example
Create BB_EnemyAI with TargetActor (Object) and TargetLocation (Vector). The perception system sets TargetActor; a custom task writes TargetLocation so Move To can use it.
Misconception

Do not use the Blackboard as a global variable store for game state. Keep it scoped and typed to avoid coupling and debugging headaches.

Key Takeaway

Blackboards let separate systems communicate with typed facts, making AI modular and testable.

Blackboard Keys (snapshot)
TargetActor — Object
Holds a reference to the player or other actors. Use an Object key with an appropriate Base Class such as Character to avoid cast errors.
TargetLocation — Vector
Stores a world position that Move To tasks can consume. Vectors are for positions and directions.
Try this
Create the Blackboard asset in the Content Browser and add the two keys above. Attach it to your Behavior Tree's Root node to make keys available.

screens.title: Creating a Blackboard and Keys
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a Blackboard is a simple, high-impact step. Start by right-clicking in the Content Browser, choose Artificial Intelligence → Blackboard, and name it BB_EnemyAI. Inside the Blackboard editor add keys for the data your AI needs. For patrol-to-chase behavior create a Vector key named TargetLocation and an Object key named TargetActor with Base Class set to Character or Actor as appropriate. Use a Boolean key for quick flags like IsPlayerDetected if you need them. Always pick the key type that matches the data you'll write; a mismatch is a common runtime error and debugging source. After adding keys, open your Behavior Tree, select the Root node, and set the Blackboard Asset to BB_EnemyAI in the Details panel. This step binds the Behavior Tree to the keys so tasks and decorators can reference them by name. A practical tip: keep names short and descriptive. TargetActor and TargetLocation are clear and make setting Blackboard values in Blueprints straightforward. Finally, confirm keys are visible in the Behavior Tree editor and try a simple manual set in Event BeginPlay for testing. What value would you store if you needed a 'last seen' location versus a 'current target'?

keyIdea.text: Make BB_EnemyAI, add typed keys, and associate the Blackboard asset with the Behavior Tree Root so keys become available at runtime.

content.html:
Process Flow

Create Blackboard & Keys

A few quick steps produce a reusable memory asset for your AI.

Steps
  1. Create a Blackboard asset in Content Browser and name it BB_EnemyAI.
  2. Add keys: Vector TargetLocation, Object TargetActor (Base Class: Character), optional Boolean IsPlayerDetected.
  3. Open Behavior Tree, select Root, set Blackboard Asset to BB_EnemyAI in Details.
  4. Verify keys appear in decorator and task property dropdowns.
Pro tip

Use descriptive names and set Base Class for Object keys to minimize casting and runtime checks.

Example key configuration
TargetActor — Object (Base: Character)
Holds the player reference for Move To (TargetActor).
TargetLocation — Vector
Holds a world position for Move To tasks that use coordinates instead of actor refs.
Why it matters

Correct keys let tasks and decorators read the precise type they expect, reducing runtime errors and simplifying behavior logic.

screens.title: Build BTT_FindPlayer — Receive Execute AI
screens.narratorSegment: A custom Behavior Tree Task lets you encapsulate the logic that finds the player and writes Blackboard values. Create a Blueprint class that inherits from BTTask_BlueprintBase and name it BTT_FindPlayer or BTT_FindPlayerAndSetBlackboard. Inside that Blueprint override Receive Execute AI. The typical flow is: Get Player Character, Cast To your player Blueprint, call Get Actor Location, then call Set Blackboard Value as Object for TargetActor and Set Blackboard Value as Vector for TargetLocation. The final and essential step is to call Finish Execute with Success set to true; forgetting Finish Execute is the most common reason tasks hang and halt the Behavior Tree. A misconception is to perform long-running logic inside the task without yielding — instead, keep tasks short or use a running state pattern and call Finish Execute later. For simple detection and updating the Blackboard, complete the updates synchronously, then Finish Execute. In testing, you can place a Delay in Event BeginPlay to set TargetActor for immediate chase while debugging. What would change if your detection system were asynchronous, like an AI Perception event? Build BTT_FindPlayer — Receive Execute AI means receive execute ai is where you write blackboard setters and must end with finish execute to resume the behavior tree.. In practical terms, blueprint logic to populate targetactor and targetlocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Task lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Receive Execute AI is where you write Blackboard setters and must end with Finish Execute to resume the Behavior Tree.

content.html:
Code WalkthroughBTT_FindPlayer

Receive Execute AI sequence

Blueprint nodes that get the player and set Blackboard values, then finish execution.

Pseudo-Blueprint flow (visualized as code)
// Event Receive Execute AI (OwnerController, ControlledPawn)
Get Player Character
Cast To ThirdPersonCharacter (As ThirdPersonCharacter)
  -> Set Blackboard Value as Object (Key: "TargetActor", Value: As ThirdPersonCharacter)
  -> Get Actor Location (Target: As ThirdPersonCharacter)
  -> Set Blackboard Value as Vector (Key: "TargetLocation", Value: Get Actor Location)
Finish Execute (Success: True)
Note the explicit Finish Execute call. Without it the tree will wait indefinitely for this task to end.
Example details
  • Use Get Player Character for single-player tests.
  • Cast to your specific player Blueprint to access Get Actor Location.
  • Use the Blackboard setter nodes that match your key types.
Pitfall: long-running logic

If your task must wait (e.g., play animations), consider using a running state pattern and call Finish Execute only when ready, otherwise keep it synchronous for simple updates.

screens.title: Blackboard Key Types
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right Blackboard Key type avoids type errors and clarifies intent. Vector keys hold positions and directions; use them for TargetLocation or LastKnownPlayerLocation. Object keys hold actor references — TargetActor is an Object key with its Base Class set to Character or Actor. Boolean keys are simple flags such as IsPlayerDetected or HasAmmo. Name keys can store labels like CurrentState when you need a small set of named states without creating an enum. A common mistake is attempting to set a vector into an object key or vice versa — Houdini-like tinkering won't help because the Behavior Tree nodes expect type alignment. When a Move To task accepts an Object key it will move to the actor's location; when it accepts a Vector key it moves to coordinates. Use Object keys when you need direct interaction with an actor (casts, calls to functions), and Vector keys when you only need a point in space. In testing, verify the set node matches the key type and the property dropdown lists the intended key. Which type would you use to store a named patrol route versus a numerical patrol index?

keyIdea.title: Match data to key types
keyIdea.text: Vectors = positions, Objects = actor refs, Booleans = flags, Names = small labels; mismatches cause runtime confusion.

content.html:
Comparison

Blackboard Key Types

Select types to match the data you will read or write.

Vector

Use for positions like TargetLocation or LastKnownPlayerLocation. Move To can consume this directly.

Object

Use for actor references like TargetActor. When you need to call functions on the actor, use Object keys and cast appropriately.

Boolean

Use for flags like IsPlayerDetected to gate Behavior Tree sequences using Blackboard decorators.

Name

Use for small labels such as CurrentState when you need simple named states without an enum.

Example

Move To (TargetActor) expects an object actor ref; Move To (TargetLocation) expects a vector. Pick the node that matches your key type.

Quick test

Attempting Set Blackboard Value as Vector on an Object key will fail or be ignored. Match types in the editor dropdowns.

screens.title: Behavior Tree: Selector and Sequence for Chase vs Patrol
screens.narratorSegment: Behavior Trees prioritize branches left-to-right inside a Selector. To make chase take precedence over patrol, structure your tree with a Selector at the Root. As the first child add a Sequence representing the chase logic. Attach a Blackboard Decorator to that Sequence and set its Key to TargetActor with Key Query set to Is Set. This decorator acts like a gate: the sequence runs only if TargetActor is populated. Inside the chase sequence place your custom BTT_FindPlayer task to update TargetActor and TargetLocation, followed by a Move To task that points to TargetActor or TargetLocation via the blackboard. Place the original patrol Sequence as the second child of the Selector so it runs only when the chase sequence fails or the decorator blocks it. This pattern ensures the AI first attempts chase when it has a target, then falls back to patrol. A common misconception is to put the decorator on the Move To node instead of the whole sequence; decorating the sequence ensures all steps that prepare and execute the chase are gated consistently. How would you extend this pattern to include a 'search last known' sequence?

keyIdea.text: Use a Root Selector with chase Sequence first (Blackboard decorator Is Set) and patrol Sequence second to prioritize chase.

content.html:
Architecture

Selector → Sequence pattern

Use a selector to choose chase first and patrol second, gated by a Blackboard decorator.

Structure
  1. Root → Selector
  2. Selector child 1 → Sequence (Chase)
    • Blackboard Decorator: TargetActor Is Set
    • Task: BTT_FindPlayer (updates keys)
    • Task: Move To (TargetActor)
  3. Selector child 2 → Sequence (Patrol) — original patrol logic
Decorator details

Use a Blackboard decorator on the chase Sequence with Key Query set to Is Set. This ensures the whole chase pipeline runs only when there is a valid TargetActor.

Why gate the sequence

Gating the sequence avoids partially executing chase logic and ensures Move To always has the data it needs.

Key Takeaway

Selectors plus Blackboard decorators provide a clear, testable priority system for AI behaviors.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Extend Patrol to Chase

Step-by-step instructions you can follow in the Editor.

Setup
  1. Create BB_EnemyAI with TargetLocation (Vector) and TargetActor (Object).
  2. Set BB_EnemyAI in BT_ThreePointPatrol Root Blackboard Asset.
Custom Task
  1. Create Blueprint class BTTask_BlueprintBase → BTT_FindPlayerAndSetBlackboard.
  2. Override Receive Execute AI and set the Blackboard keys, then Finish Execute.
Behavior Tree
  1. Add chase Sequence as first child of Selector with Blackboard decorator TargetActor Is Set.
  2. Insert BTT_FindPlayerAndSetBlackboard and Move To(TargetActor) inside that Sequence.
Quick test steps
  • In AI Controller Event BeginPlay, after Run Behavior Tree add Delay(2s), then Set Blackboard Value as Object to Get Player Character for testing.
  • Play in Editor and open the Behavior Tree debugger to watch keys update.
If the AI doesn't chase

screens.title: Finish Execute and runtime stalls
screens.narratorSegment: Finish Execute is the final signal a custom Behavior Tree Task must send to return control to the tree. When you call Receive Execute AI you start a task's work. If you never call Finish Execute the tree will wait forever, making the AI appear frozen or stuck on that node. This is often confusing because the Blueprint appears to run but the Behavior Tree debugger shows the task still active. Another common source of stalls is executing lengthy blocking operations inside Receive Execute AI: long waits, heavy loops, or blocking input and output. The correct pattern for long work is to either split the task into start and completion phases, use timers or latent actions, or use the task's running state and call Finish Execute only once the asynchronous work completes. When diagnosing a stall, first inspect your custom task and ensure every execution path ends with Finish Execute. Add logging or prints to the start and end of the task when you test in PIE. The core rule: a task must explicitly tell the tree when it's done; without that, the Behavior Tree cannot make progress. keyIdea.text: Call Finish Execute on every execution path; use timers or running-state patterns for delayed completion to avoid stalls.

content.html:
Common Mistakes

Finish Execute and stalls

Why tasks hang and how to fix them.

Problem

A custom task runs but the Behavior Tree never moves on because Finish Execute was not called or execution took too long synchronously.

Diagnosis steps
  • Add print or log at the start and before Finish Execute.
  • Check for branches that skip Finish Execute on error conditions.
  • Ensure no blocking loops or waits are performed synchronously.
Solution patterns
  1. Use timers or Delays and call Finish Execute when the timer fires.
  2. Use a running state and handle completion in Event Tick or callbacks.
  3. Keep short, synchronous tasks simple and call Finish Execute immediately after updates.
Key Takeaway

Every BTTask must explicitly call Finish Execute to allow the tree to progress; plan for long work using timers or running-state patterns.

screens.title: Blackboard Decorators for gating behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Blackboard Decorators are lightweight checks attached to Behavior Tree nodes that evaluate Blackboard Keys. A commonly used check is Is Set, which tests whether an Object or Vector key contains a value. Use Is Set on your chase Sequence to require a valid TargetActor before attempting chase. Other queries include Equals or Not Equals for comparing Name or Boolean keys. A common misconception is to decorate a single task like Move To instead of the whole Sequence; decorating the Sequence ensures that tasks that prepare data and tasks that act on it are only executed when the key state is correct. Decorators can be combined with Services for periodic updates, or with conditioned sequences that clear keys when conditions fail. When designing decorators, think in terms of preconditions for behavior: what must be true for this branch to make sense? For example, require TargetActor Is Set and HasLineOfSight true before starting an attack sequence. In many projects you will add a short wait or validation task that populates or validates Blackboard entries before a heavy action executes. What preconditions would you add to avoid chasing to invalid locations?

content.html:
Decorator Use

Blackboard Decorators as Preconditions

Decorators gate sequences and protect tasks from invalid data.

Common decorator queries
  • Is Set — checks existence
  • Equals / Not Equals — compare Name or Boolean
  • Custom conditions combined with Services for periodic checks
Example: Chase preconditions
Attach a Blackboard decorator to the chase Sequence: TargetActor Is Set. Optionally add a HasLineOfSight decorator or a boolean check to confirm perception validity before attempting chase.
Design tip

Decorators should express what must be true, not how to compute it. Use tasks or services to compute and populate keys, and decorators to check them.

Key Takeaway

Decorators form the precondition layer that keeps sequences safe and predictable; compute values in tasks and validate them with decorators.

screens.title: Debugging Blackboard Values in PIE
screens.narratorSegment: Inspecting Blackboard values in Play-In-Editor is the fastest way to confirm your AI is working. Run the game in PIE and open the Behavior Tree editor. The Blackboard debugger panel shows keys and their runtime values per AI Controller. Watch TargetActor and TargetLocation change as your custom task sets them. Add print statements in your custom task to confirm Receive Execute AI and Finish Execute are invoked. screens.title: Assessment: Remembering the last seen location
screens.narratorSegment: A practical assessment asks you to implement a 'remember last known location' behavior. The Blackboard part requires a Vector key, LastKnownPlayerLocation. You will author a custom task, BTT_UpdateLastKnownPlayerLocation, whose Receive Execute AI logic gets the player character, gets their actor location, and sets the Blackboard Vector key LastKnownPlayerLocation. Call Finish Execute when done. Integrate this task into a Sequence that runs while the player is visible, and when the player is no longer visible have a decorator check Is Set on LastKnownPlayerLocation to run a Move To task that examines the last known spot. A common misunderstanding is to rely solely on perception without persisting a last known value; storing the vector lets the AI navigate to where it last saw the player even if perception drops. For evaluation, run a scenario where the player briefly appears then hides, and verify the AI moves to LastKnownPlayerLocation and then resumes patrol if nothing is found. Assessment Idea

Remember Last Known Location

Design a Blackboard key and a task to persist where the player was last seen, then use it to investigate.

Implementation outline
  1. Add Vector key: LastKnownPlayerLocation to BB_EnemyAI.
  2. Create BTT_UpdateLastKnownPlayerLocation: Get Player Character → Get Actor Location → Set Blackboard Value as Vector → Finish Execute.
  3. Run this task when the player is visible; when not visible check LastKnownPlayerLocation Is Set and Move To that vector.
Evaluation

Test a scenario where the player appears and then hides. Confirm the AI uses LastKnownPlayerLocation to investigate, then clears the key or resumes patrol when nothing is found.

Key Takeaway

Persisting last known vectors makes behavior realistic and gives you a clear hook for investigation logic.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we will take a patrol AI that feels rigid and make it responsive. The Blackboard is the AI's short-term memory — a shared place where the AI Controller, Behavior Tree, and perception systems store the values that matter in the moment, like a target actor or a target location. You'll learn how Blackboard Keys represent typed variables such as Vector, Object, Boolean, and Name, and why choosing the right key type matters. We'll also build a custom Behavior Tree Task in Blueprint that finds the player, writes their actor and location into the Blackboard, and then finishes cleanly so the Behavior Tree can continue. Finally, we'll modify a Behavior Tree to prioritize chasing the player using a Selector and a Blackboard decorator that checks if a target is set. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to create BB_EnemyAI, add keys, author a BTTask_BlueprintBase to update the Blackboard, and wire a chase-vs-patrol selector so AI behaves more naturally. Think about how a shared memory helps different systems coordinate without tight coupling — that's the core idea you'll use repeatedly.

By the end of this chapter you will understand why the Blackboard is the central shared memory for AI and how Blackboard Keys let you store typed facts like positions, actor references, and boolean states. You will be able to create and wire a Blackboard asset to a Behavior Tree, select the correct key types for your data, and use them inside tasks and decorators. You will also author custom Behavior Tree Tasks in Blueprint, implement their logic in Receive Execute AI, and correctly call Finish Execute so the tree continues. Finally, you will integrate these pieces to build a chase priority: the AI checks for a target, runs a custom task to populate Blackboard entries, then moves to the target; when the target is absent the AI resumes patrol. Each objective includes a brief competency milestone so you can confirm mastery by inspection and runtime testing. These skills will make your AI modular, debuggable, and ready for more advanced perception systems later on.

These learning objectives focus on practical verification and common mistakes. You should be able to create BB_EnemyAI with keys named TargetLocation and TargetActor, attach it to BT_Patrol or BT_ThreePointPatrol, and observe values updating in the Blackboard debugger. You will also author a custom task, for example BTT_FindPlayer, that obtains the player reference and location and writes them to the proper keys. A key verification step is to test that the custom task calls Finish Execute; missing this call is the most common cause of a Behavior Tree hanging. Another common mistake is choosing the wrong key type — trying to set a vector into an object key will cause runtime confusion. The objective here is not just to build, but to test in PIE: run the Behavior Tree, open the Behavior Tree and Blackboard debugger, and confirm the selector prioritizes chase when TargetActor is set. These steps establish both correctness and debugging confidence.

The Blackboard is best understood as a short-term memory store for an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree. It is an asset you create in the Content Browser, then populate with keys that describe facts the AI might need right now: where to move, which actor to chase, or whether a state flag is set. The power of the Blackboard comes from decoupling: perception components, tasks, decorators, and other Blueprints can all read from and write to the same set of keys without calling each other directly. For example, a perception component can set a TargetActor key when it sees the player; a custom task can later read that key and write TargetLocation; a Move To task can then use TargetLocation or TargetActor. A common misconception is to treat the Blackboard like a global game state — instead, treat it as short-lived, local memory scoped to an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree. Use clear naming and correct key types to avoid confusion. In practice, you'll create BB_EnemyAI, add Vector and Object keys, attach it to your Behavior Tree root, and then watch values change in the debugger as runtime evidence that systems are communicating correctly. How might you limit what you store in the Blackboard to avoid clutter?

Creating a Blackboard is a simple, high-impact step. Start by right-clicking in the Content Browser, choose Artificial Intelligence → Blackboard, and name it BB_EnemyAI. Inside the Blackboard editor add keys for the data your AI needs. For patrol-to-chase behavior create a Vector key named TargetLocation and an Object key named TargetActor with Base Class set to Character or Actor as appropriate. Use a Boolean key for quick flags like IsPlayerDetected if you need them. Always pick the key type that matches the data you'll write; a mismatch is a common runtime error and debugging source. After adding keys, open your Behavior Tree, select the Root node, and set the Blackboard Asset to BB_EnemyAI in the Details panel. This step binds the Behavior Tree to the keys so tasks and decorators can reference them by name. A practical tip: keep names short and descriptive. TargetActor and TargetLocation are clear and make setting Blackboard values in Blueprints straightforward. Finally, confirm keys are visible in the Behavior Tree editor and try a simple manual set in Event BeginPlay for testing. What value would you store if you needed a 'last seen' location versus a 'current target'?

A custom Behavior Tree Task lets you encapsulate the logic that finds the player and writes Blackboard values. Create a Blueprint class that inherits from BTTask_BlueprintBase and name it BTT_FindPlayer or BTT_FindPlayerAndSetBlackboard. Inside that Blueprint override Receive Execute AI. The typical flow is: Get Player Character, Cast To your player Blueprint, call Get Actor Location, then call Set Blackboard Value as Object for TargetActor and Set Blackboard Value as Vector for TargetLocation. The final and essential step is to call Finish Execute with Success set to true; forgetting Finish Execute is the most common reason tasks hang and halt the Behavior Tree. A misconception is to perform long-running logic inside the task without yielding — instead, keep tasks short or use a running state pattern and call Finish Execute later. In testing, you can place a Delay in Event BeginPlay to set TargetActor for immediate chase while debugging. What would change if your detection system were asynchronous, like an AI Perception event? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right Blackboard Key type avoids type errors and clarifies intent. Vector keys hold positions and directions; use them for TargetLocation or LastKnownPlayerLocation. Object keys hold actor references — TargetActor is an Object key with its Base Class set to Character or Actor. Boolean keys are simple flags such as IsPlayerDetected or HasAmmo. When a Move To task accepts an Object key it will move to the actor's location; when it accepts a Vector key it moves to coordinates. Use Object keys when you need direct interaction with an actor (casts, calls to functions), and Vector keys when you only need a point in space. In testing, verify the set node matches the key type and the property dropdown lists the intended key. Which type would you use to store a named patrol route versus a numerical patrol index?

Behavior Trees prioritize branches left-to-right inside a Selector. To make chase take precedence over patrol, structure your tree with a Selector at the Root.
